title: Apple iPhone Duo Cracks After 75,000 Real‑World Folds, Gizmodo Reports】
body:
Apple’s latest fold‑able, the iPhone Duo, has reportedly failed after just 75,000 opening and closing cycles in an independent durability test, raising questions about the company’s transparency and the long‑term viability of its new form factor. While Apple has highlighted the Duo’s sleek design, advanced camera system and seamless software integration, it omitted a key specification that rivals routinely disclose: the number of folds the device can endure before mechanical failure. The omission, coupled with the premature breakage, could affect consumer confidence and give competitors a strategic edge in the rapidly expanding fold‑able market.

The test, conducted by a third‑party lab that specializes in durability assessments for mobile devices, involved repeatedly opening and closing the Duo’s hinge mechanism at a rate of roughly 100 cycles per hour. After 75,000 cycles—equivalent to about three years of typical daily use—the central hinge exhibited a micro‑fracture that caused the display to delaminate, rendering the screen unusable. By comparison, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series and Huawei’s Mate X line have historically been rated for 200,000 to 300,000 cycles, with manufacturers openly advertising these figures as a testament to engineering robustness.

Apple’s silence on the fold‑count metric is notable because it diverges from an industry norm that has become a selling point for fold‑able devices. When Samsung unveiled its first foldable, it emphasized a “200,000‑fold” guarantee, and Huawei followed suit with similar claims. Analysts suggest that Apple’s decision to withhold this data may be strategic, aiming to avoid setting a benchmark that could be challenged by early‑stage hardware limitations. However, the lack of transparency can also be interpreted as a reluctance to acknowledge potential durability concerns, especially given the premium price tag attached to the Duo.

Industry experts are divided on the implications of the test results. Some argue that the 75,000‑fold figure, while lower than competitors’, still represents a respectable lifespan for a device expected to be replaced within a typical three‑to‑four‑year upgrade cycle. Others contend that the early failure highlights a fundamental engineering hurdle: the stress placed on ultra‑thin glass and hinge components when repeatedly folded. “Apple’s approach to foldables appears to prioritize aesthetics and software integration over mechanical endurance,” said Lina Patel, a senior analyst at TechInsights. “If the hardware cannot match the durability expectations set by the market, the overall user experience will suffer, regardless of how smooth the UI feels.”

The durability debate also intersects with broader consumer trends. Fold‑able smartphones have struggled to achieve mainstream adoption, partly due to high costs and lingering doubts about long‑term reliability. Apple’s entry into the segment was seen as a potential catalyst for wider acceptance, leveraging its brand loyalty and ecosystem. Yet the recent findings may reinforce existing hesitations. Retailers have already reported a cautious response to the Duo, with pre‑order numbers lagging behind projections for other flagship releases. Moreover, warranty claims related to hinge failures could strain Apple’s service infrastructure, especially if the issue proves more widespread than the lab test suggests.

Looking ahead, Apple is expected to address durability concerns through both hardware refinements and clearer communication. Rumors indicate that the next iteration of the Duo could feature a reinforced hinge, a more resilient polymer‑based display substrate, and an official fold‑count rating backed by internal testing. Such moves would align Apple with industry standards and reassure potential buyers. In the meantime, the current episode serves as a reminder that innovation in fold‑able technology remains a balancing act between cutting‑edge design and the practical demands of everyday use. Consumers and investors will be watching closely to see whether Apple can close the durability gap and deliver a truly resilient fold‑able experience.
